claim: Spiny projection neurons (SPNs) in the dorsal striatum play crucial roles in locomotion control and value-based decision-making.
source: Spiny projection neurons (SPNs) in the dorsal striatum play crucial roles in locomotion control and value-based decision-making.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about SPNs.

claim: SPNs include both direct-pathway striatonigral and indirect-pathway striatopallidal neurons.
source: SPNs, which include both direct-pathway striatonigral and indirect-pathway striatopallidal neurons, can be further classified into subtypes based on distinct transcriptomic profiles and cell body distribution patterns.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about striatal neuron classification.

claim: SPNs can be further classified into subtypes based on distinct transcriptomic profiles and cell body distribution patterns.
source: SPNs, which include both direct-pathway striatonigral and indirect-pathway striatopallidal neurons, can be further classified into subtypes based on distinct transcriptomic profiles and cell body distribution patterns.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about SPN classification methods.

claim: Sepw1-Cre transgenic mice label a specific SPN subtype characterized by a patchy distribution of cell bodies in the dorsal striatum.
source: Using Sepw1-Cre transgenic mice, which label a specific SPN subtype characterized by a patchy distribution of cell bodies in the dorsal striatum, we found that these patchy striatonigral neurons constrain motor vigor in response to valence differentials.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior characterization of this mouse line and confirmed by histological data in the manuscript.

claim: Patchy striatonigral neurons constrain motor vigor in response to valence differentials.
source: Using Sepw1-Cre transgenic mice, which label a specific SPN subtype characterized by a patchy distribution of cell bodies in the dorsal striatum, we found that these patchy striatonigral neurons constrain motor vigor in response to valence differentials.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by multiple experimental manipulations including ablation, chemogenetics, and optogenetics described in the manuscript.

claim: Mice exhibited differential walking speeds between the light and dark zones in a modified light/dark box test.
source: In a modified light/dark box test, mice exhibited differential walking speeds between the light and dark zones.
evidence: This is directly supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: Genetic ablation of patchy SPNs disrupted restful slowing in the dark zone.
source: Genetic ablation of these patchy SPNs disrupted restful slowing in the dark zone and increased zone discrimination by speed.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1H showing reduced time at low speeds in the dark zone for PA mice.

claim: Genetic ablation of patchy SPNs increased zone discrimination by speed.
source: Genetic ablation of these patchy SPNs disrupted restful slowing in the dark zone and increased zone discrimination by speed.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1J showing increased BIL effect on transition speed in PA mice.

claim: In vivo recordings linked the activity of patchy neurons to zone occupancy, speed, and deceleration.
source: In vivo recordings linked the activity of these neurons to zone occupancy, speed, and deceleration, with a specific role in mediating deceleration.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Patchy neurons have a specific role in mediating deceleration.
source: In vivo recordings linked the activity of these neurons to zone occupancy, speed, and deceleration, with a specific role in mediating deceleration.
evidence: This is supported by ROC analysis showing strong deceleration prediction (Figure 2L) and cross-correlation analysis (Figures 3G, 4H).

claim: Chemogenetic activation of patchy SPNs reduced locomotion.
source: Furthermore, chemogenetic activation of patchy SPNs—and optical activation of striatonigral neurons in particular—reduced locomotion and attenuated speed-based zone discrimination.
evidence: This is supported by DREADD experiments shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Optical activation of striatonigral neurons reduced locomotion.
source: Furthermore, chemogenetic activation of patchy SPNs—and optical activation of striatonigral neurons in particular—reduced locomotion and attenuated speed-based zone discrimination.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of patchy SPNs attenuated speed-based zone discrimination.
source: Furthermore, chemogenetic activation of patchy SPNs—and optical activation of striatonigral neurons in particular—reduced locomotion and attenuated speed-based zone discrimination.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5J showing reduced BIL effect on transition speed in Gq mice.

claim: Optical activation of striatonigral neurons attenuated speed-based zone discrimination.
source: Furthermore, chemogenetic activation of patchy SPNs—and optical activation of striatonigral neurons in particular—reduced locomotion and attenuated speed-based zone discrimination.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6I showing reduced BIL effect on transition speed in ChR mice.

claim: A subtype of patchy striatonigral neurons regulates implicit walking speed selection based on innate valence differentials.
source: These findings reveal that a subtype of patchy striatonigral neurons regulates implicit walking speed selection based on innate valence differentials.
evidence: This is the main conclusion synthesized from all experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: Motor control relies on the complementary and simultaneous regulation of downstream nuclei by the striatal direct and indirect pathways.
source: Motor control relies on the complementary and simultaneous regulation of downstream nuclei by the striatal direct and indirect pathways (Kravitz et al., 2010; Cui et al., 2013; Barbera et al., 2016; Yttri and Dudman, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Striatal projection neurons (SPNs) are hypothesized to encode implicit motivation through the regulation of action vigor, such as movement speed.
source: Striatal projection neurons (SPNs) are further hypothesized to encode implicit motivation through the regulation of action vigor, such as movement speed (Dudman and Krakauer, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: The mechanisms by which striatal microcircuitry achieves regulation of action vigor remain poorly understood.
source: However, the mechanisms by which striatal microcircuitry achieves this remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A subpopulation of SPNs, referred to as 'patch' or 'striosome' neurons, is organized into distinct patchy clusters of varying sizes within the broader striatal matrix.
source: A subpopulation of SPNs, referred to as 'patch' or 'striosome' neurons, is organized into distinct patchy clusters of varying sizes within the broader striatal matrix (Crittenden and Graybiel, 2011; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: Both patch and matrix compartments comprise a mixture of direct and indirect pathway SPNs.
source: Both patch and matrix compartments comprise a mixture of direct and indirect pathway SPNs (Crittenden and Graybiel, 2011; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: Differences in neurochemical and genetic composition, along with distinct interactions with surrounding circuitry, suggest that patch and matrix territories have specialized roles in regulating behavior.
source: Despite this similarity, differences in neurochemical and genetic composition, along with distinct interactions with surrounding circuitry, suggest that patch and matrix territories have specialized roles in regulating behavior (Graybiel and Matsushima, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Recent behavioral studies highlight the unique roles of patchy SPNs, implicating them in value-based learning and risk assessment.
source: Recent behavioral studies highlight the unique roles of patchy SPNs, implicating them in value-based learning and risk assessment (Friedman et al., 2015; Friedman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: The interplay between valuative functions and the conventional role of the striatum in locomotor control remains poorly understood.
source: However, the interplay between these valuative functions and the conventional role of the striatum in locomotor control remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Patchy SPNs are a compelling candidate for linking external valence to implicit motivational processes, such as action vigor and movement speed.
source: Given their distinctive characteristics, patchy SPNs are a compelling candidate for linking external valence to implicit motivational processes, such as action vigor and movement speed.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from known characteristics of patchy SPNs.

claim: Patchy SPNs are themselves diverse.
source: Studies of patchy SPNs make it clear these neurons are themselves diverse, and that accessing this population in varied ways necessarily results in the study of various subpopulations.
evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Patchy SPNs were first distinguished from the surrounding matrix based on gradients in histochemical markers.
source: Patchy SPNs were first distinguished from the surrounding matrix based on gradients in histochemical markers (Pert et al., 1976; Gerfen, 1984; Graybiel, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical anatomical studies.

claim: Patchy SPNs have been accessed in vivo by relying on prenatal injections, by targeting patchy SPN-preferring afferents, and through the development of genetically modified mouse lines.
source: They have since been accessed in vivo by relying on prenatal injections, by targeting patchy SPN-preferring afferents, and most recently through the development of genetically modified mouse lines with transgene expression controlled by genes concentrated in patchy SPNs (Brimblecombe and Cragg, 2017; Prager and Plotkin, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to methodological studies.

claim: The Sepw1-Cre (NP67) BAC transgenic line was selected to label patchy SPNs.
source: For the present study, we selected the Sepw1-Cre (NP67) BAC transgenic line to label the patchy SPNs (Gerfen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological choice supported by citation.

claim: Patchy SPNs in Sepw1-Cre mice include both direct (80%) and indirect (20%) pathway neurons.
source: These patchy SPNs include both direct (80%) and indirect (20%) pathway neurons and, unlike the matrix, receive innervation by the anxiety-modulating bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior characterization study.

claim: Patchy SPNs in Sepw1-Cre mice receive innervation by the anxiety-modulating bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, unlike the matrix.
source: These patchy SPNs include both direct (80%) and indirect (20%) pathway neurons and, unlike the matrix, receive innervation by the anxiety-modulating bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior anatomical study.

claim: The Sepw1-Cre line expresses Cre in roughly 15% of striatal territory.
source: This line is well characterized to express Cre in roughly 15% of striatal territory, representing similar striatal coverage to that derived from classic histological characterization of patchy SPNs (Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior characterization study.

claim: The Sepw1-Cre line represents similar striatal coverage to that derived from classic histological characterization of patchy SPNs.
source: This line is well characterized to express Cre in roughly 15% of striatal territory, representing similar striatal coverage to that derived from classic histological characterization of patchy SPNs (Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior characterization study.

claim: Patchy SPNs control the speed at which mice navigate the valence differential between high- and low-anxiety zones, without affecting valence perception itself.
source: Our findings reveal that patchy SPNs control the speed at which mice navigate the valence differential between high- and low-anxiety zones, without affecting valence perception itself.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by behavioral data showing preserved zone preference but altered speed profiles.

claim: This provides the first evidence that patchy SPNs regulate naturalistic motor behavior.
source: This provides the first evidence that patchy SPNs regulate naturalistic motor behavior and demonstrate that they drive implicit motivation to align situational valence with speed selection.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Patchy SPNs drive implicit motivation to align situational valence with speed selection.
source: This provides the first evidence that patchy SPNs regulate naturalistic motor behavior and demonstrate that they drive implicit motivation to align situational valence with speed selection.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by the totality of experimental findings.

claim: Cre-dependent mCherry signals were colocalized with the patch marker µ-opioid receptor (MOR1) in the dorsal striatum of control mice.
source: Cre-dependent mCherry signals were colocalized with the patch marker µ-opioid receptor (MOR1) in the dorsal striatum of controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PA mice showed an approximately 60% loss of patchy neurons in the dorsal striatum compared to control mice.
source: Examination of MOR1-positive territories following behavior revealed an approximately 60% loss of patchy neurons in the dorsal striatum of PA mice compared to control mice (p<0.0001, Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of MOR1 staining shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No loss of MOR1-positive territories was observed in the ventral striatum of either PA or control mice.
source: By contrast, no loss of MOR1-positive territories was observed in the ventral striatum of either PA or control mice (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of MOR1 staining shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Control mice demonstrated dark preference through greater stay time in the dark zone.
source: Behavior in control mice verified dark preference, as demonstrated by greater stay time in the dark zone.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: PA mice demonstrated dark preference through greater stay time in the dark zone.
source: Similar to controls, PA mice also demonstrated dark preference through greater stay time in the dark zone (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Speed was higher during exploration of the anxiogenic light zone for both control and PA mice.
source: Speed was higher during exploration of the anxiogenic light zone for both control and PA mice, despite higher dark zone speed following ablation (L vs D control p=0.001, PA p=0.0371; control vs PA in dark p=0.0015, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Dark zone speed was higher for PA mice than for control mice.
source: Speed was higher during exploration of the anxiogenic light zone for both control and PA mice, despite higher dark zone speed following ablation (L vs D control p=0.001, PA p=0.0371; control vs PA in dark p=0.0015, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The similarity of PA mice to controls in terms of dark preference and relatively greater light zone speed indicates that patch SPNs are not critical for basic discrimination of situational valence.
source: The similarity of PA mice to controls in terms of dark preference and relatively greater light zone speed indicates that patch SPNs are not critical for basic discrimination of situational valence.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data showing preserved zone preference and light/dark speed differences.

claim: Average speed in the dark zones was higher for PA mice than for control mice.
source: While zone preference was normal, average speed in the dark zones and the maximum speed obtained were higher for PA mice than for control mice (dark zone speed p=0.0015, max speed p=0.0434, Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Maximum speed obtained was higher for PA mice than for control mice.
source: While zone preference was normal, average speed in the dark zones and the maximum speed obtained were higher for PA mice than for control mice (dark zone speed p=0.0015, max speed p=0.0434, Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The reflection of valence in speed distributions between light and dark zones, present in controls, was lost for PA mice.
source: Importantly, the reflection of valence in speed distributions between light and dark zones, present in controls, was lost for PA mice.
evidence: This is supported by speed distribution data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: PA mice showed a significant reduction in the percent time spent at restful speeds (≤2 cm/s) in the dark zones relative to controls.
source: The loss was due to a significant reduction in the percent time spent at restful speeds (≤2 cm/s) in the dark zones among PA mice relative to controls (p=0.0018, Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by speed distribution data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Reduced stillness in the dark zones suggests that ablation of patchy SPNs leads to a failure to slow down or rest under safe conditions.
source: Given that PA mice retained zone discrimination and dark preference, reduced stillness in the dark zones suggests that ablation of patchy SPNs leads to a failure to slow down or rest under safe conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: Zone transitions were accompanied by speed peaks for all mice.
source: Zone transitions were accompanied by speed peaks for all mice (Figure 1I), suggesting invigorated action selection at this choice point.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Speed peaks at zone transitions suggest invigorated action selection at this choice point.
source: Zone transitions were accompanied by speed peaks for all mice (Figure 1I), suggesting invigorated action selection at this choice point.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed speed peaks.

claim: For controls, differential speed due to surrounding valence is immediately apparent at the moment of transition, with greater speeds expressed on either side of a transition accompanying body-in-light versus body-in-dark moments.
source: For controls, differential speed due to surrounding valence is immediately apparent in this moment of transition, with greater speeds expressed on either side of a transition accompanying the body-in-light (BIL, i.e. preceding a transition into dark and following a transition into light) versus body-in-dark (BID) moments.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Both factors of BIL and PA mice were shown to increase speed at the transition choice point.
source: Both factors of BIL and PA mice were shown to increase speed at this choice point (GLME coefficient fixed effects 95% CI for speed increase by PA [0.73218, 3.9241] and BIL [1.7464, 2.3911] on approach, or by PA [2.2344, 2.8761], and BIL [0.89109, 3.593] on retreat).
evidence: This is supported by GLME analysis of transition speed data.

claim: PA mice responded to a shift in valence accompanying zone transitions with acutely elevated speed during BIL windows.
source: As with controls, PA mice responded to a shift in valence accompanying zone transitions with acutely elevated speed during BIL windows.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: BIL had a larger effect on transition speed for PA mice than for controls.
source: However, BIL had a larger effect on transition speed for PA mice than for controls, indicating that PA mice exhibited elevated transition discrimination through velocity (GLME fixed effects 95% CI for impact of BIL on speed: PA approach [2.3376 3.347], retreat [3.2809, 4.2788]; control approach [0.9698, 1.7612], retreat [1.0784, 1.8056], Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by GLME analysis shown in Figure 1J.

claim: PA mice exhibited elevated transition discrimination through velocity.
source: However, BIL had a larger effect on transition speed for PA mice than for controls, indicating that PA mice exhibited elevated transition discrimination through velocity (GLME fixed effects 95% CI for impact of BIL on speed: PA approach [2.3376 3.347], retreat [3.2809, 4.2788]; control approach [0.9698, 1.7612], retreat [1.0784, 1.8056], Figure 1J).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GLME analysis results.

claim: The pattern of excess speed in PA mice suggests that patchy SPNs naturally lower speed, supporting rest in the dark and alleviating anxious vigor surrounding transitions.
source: Collectively, the pattern of excess speed in PA mice suggests that patchy SPNs naturally lower speed, supporting rest in the dark and alleviating anxious vigor surrounding transitions.
evidence: This is an interpretation synthesizing multiple behavioral findings.

claim: No substantial difference existed between LLb and DDb performance in terms of average or maximum speed for either group.
source: We found no substantial difference between LLb from DDb performance in terms of average or maximum speed for either group (Figure 1L–M).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1L-M.

claim: No difference in speed distribution between LLb and DDb was apparent.
source: Moreover, no difference in speed distribution between LLb and DDb was apparent (Figure 1N).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1N.

claim: Local speed peaks persisted while transitioning between equally illuminated zones.
source: Local speed peaks persisted while transitioning between equally illuminated zones, perhaps due to the decision to turn a corner or pass through a relatively constricted point joining larger rooms.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1O.

claim: Transition speeds did not differ between LLb and DDb.
source: Yet these transition speeds did not differ between LLb and DDb (Figure 1O–P, 'BIA' denotes body in start side 'A,' analogous to BIL as mice are started in LDb light).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1O-P.

claim: The zone-specific LDb speed profile is not related simply to light level but is dependent on a light versus dark valence differential.
source: Thus, the zone-specific LDb speed profile is not related simply to light level but is dependent on a light versus dark valence differential.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of LDb to LLb/DDb results.

claim: The LLb/DDb data help to establish LDb speed as a behavioral reflection of differential situational valence.
source: Therefore, the LLb/DDb data help to establish LDb speed as a behavioral reflection of differential situational valence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the LLb/DDb control experiments.

claim: PA elevates valence-specific speed without inducing general hyperactivity.
source: These data also indicate that PA elevates valence-specific speed without inducing general hyperactivity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of LDb to LLb/DDb results.

claim: Locomotor speed modulation by Sepw1+ patchy neurons depends on the presence of a salient valence differential.
source: Collectively, these data show that locomotor speed modulation by Sepw1+ patchy neurons depends on the presence of a salient valence differential.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the LDb and LLb/DDb experiments.

claim: A majority of Sepw1-Cre positive patchy SPNs are the direct-pathway neurons known for promoting locomotion.
source: A majority of Sepw1-Cre positive patchy SPNs are the direct-pathway neurons known for promoting locomotion (Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior characterization study.

claim: Ablation of patchy SPNs increased speed during LDb navigation, indicating an inhibitory role of patchy SPNs in regulating locomotion.
source: However, we found that ablation of patchy SPNs increased speed during LDb navigation (Figure 1F and G), indicating an inhibitory role of patchy SPNs in regulating locomotion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ablation experiment results.

claim: Histology following GCaMP6s transduction and behavior confirmed 1 mm diameter GRIN lens position on the top of GCaMP-positive patchy neurons in the dorsal striatum.
source: Histology following GCaMP6s transduction and behavior confirmed 1 mm diameter GRIN lens position on the top of GCaMP-positive patchy neurons in the dorsal striatum (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The 10 imaged mice demonstrated the LDb speed phenotype consistent with controls in the ablation experiment.
source: Aside from a lack of separation in speeds approaching transitions (possibly due to burden of miniscope wearing), the 10 imaged mice demonstrated the LDb speed phenotype consistent with controls in our ablation experiment (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-I).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-I.

claim: Neurons showing preferential activation in the light zone substantially outnumbered neurons preferentially active in the dark zone.
source: Neurons showing preferential activation in the light zone substantially outnumbered neurons preferentially active in the dark zone (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Striatal neurons display heterogeneous responses to movement speed, exhibiting both linear and nonlinear relationships.
source: A recent study showed that striatal neurons display heterogeneous responses to movement speed, exhibiting both linear and nonlinear relationships (Fobbs et al., 2020; Dong et al., 2025).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Speed-tuned cell subtypes with both linear (positive L+ and negative L-) and quadratic (positive Q+ and negative Q-) speed-tuning profiles were identified.
source: Similarly, we identified speed-tuned cell subtypes with both linear (positive L+ and negative L-) and quadratic (positive Q+ and negative Q-) speed-tuning profiles (Figure 2G and H; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: Approximately 53% of neurons demonstrated speed-activity relationships (L+, L-, Q+, and Q-).
source: Approximately 53% of neurons demonstrated such speed-activity relationships (L+, L-, Q+, and Q-), with the largest fraction of speed-related cells having a quadratic negative relationship (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The largest fraction of speed-related cells had a quadratic negative relationship.
source: Approximately 53% of neurons demonstrated such speed-activity relationships (L+, L-, Q+, and Q-), with the largest fraction of speed-related cells having a quadratic negative relationship (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: 76% of neurons could be defined by relationships to zone and/or speed.
source: Collectively, 76% of neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J) could be defined by these relationships to zone and/or speed, and the distribution of neurons among these categories was highly consistent across mice (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J.

claim: The distribution of neurons among zone and/or speed categories was highly consistent across mice.
source: Collectively, 76% of neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J) could be defined by these relationships to zone and/or speed, and the distribution of neurons among these categories was highly consistent across mice (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2I and J.

claim: Light preference and speed relationships coincided within neurons more often than predicted by chance.
source: Light preference and speed relationships coincided within neurons more often than predicted by chance (χ2 (3, n=532)=78.63, p<0.0001, Figure 2—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K.

claim: More than half of light-related neurons possess a Q- relationship to speed.
source: Interestingly, more than half of light-related neurons possess a Q-relationship to speed (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Many patchy neurons are engaged in speed modulation, particularly within the anxiogenic light.
source: These data suggest that many patchy neurons are engaged in speed modulation, particularly within the anxiogenic light.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the calcium imaging data.

claim: For most patchy neurons, a strong relationship between deceleration and calcium activity was found.
source: For most patchy neurons, we found a strong relationship between deceleration and calcium activity, represented through acceleration/deceleration preference index (ADI) (computed with area under ROC curve, see Materials and methods) values close to –1 (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by ROC analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Neurons for which no speed or zone relationship could be identified were disproportionately apt to be DP cells.
source: Those neurons for which we had been unable to identify a speed or zone relationship were disproportionately apt to be DP cells (χ2(1,1565)=24.33, p<0.0001, Figure 2M), providing for categorization of additional neurons.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2M.

claim: A significant relationship to some combination of zone, speed, or deceleration could be ascribed to approximately 98% (1531 of 1565 neurons) of imaged patchy neurons.
source: As a result, we were able to ascribe a significant relationship to some combination of zone, speed, or deceleration to approximately 98% (1531 of 1565 neurons) of imaged patchy neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the calcium imaging analysis results.

claim: These data corroborate the finding that ablation of patchy neurons increased speed at select moments in the LDbox by showing that many imaged patchy neurons act in concert with locomotor deceleration.
source: Importantly, these data corroborate our finding that ablation of patchy neurons increased speed at select moments in the LDbox by showing that many imaged patchy neurons act in concert with locomotor deceleration.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the calcium imaging results to the ablation results.

claim: A significant interaction existed between transition-active status and zone/speed relationships.
source: We found a significant interaction between transition-active status and zone/speed relationships (χ2(4, n=1565)=137.3, p<0.0001, Figure 3A) such that cells jointly encoding both light and speed were most abundant among transition-active neurons.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cells jointly encoding both light and speed were most abundant among transition-active neurons.
source: We found a significant interaction between transition-active status and zone/speed relationships (χ2(4, n=1565)=137.3, p<0.0001, Figure 3A) such that cells jointly encoding both light and speed were most abundant among transition-active neurons.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Purely speed-related cells, dark and speed-related cells, and cells with no identified zone or speed relationship were most abundant among neurons not active at transitions.
source: Meanwhile, purely speed-related cells, dark and speed-related cells, and cells with no identified zone or speed relationship were most abundant among neurons not active at transitions.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The most common speed relationship remained quadratic-negative among transition-active neurons.
source: The most common speed relationship remained quadratic-negative among transition-active neurons, like all neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J, L).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J, L.

claim: Deceleration prediction disproportionately characterized neurons not active at transition.
source: While deceleration prediction disproportionately characterized neurons not active at transition (χ2(1, n=1565)=24.33, p<0.0001, Figure 3B), most transition-active neurons were also DP (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Most transition-active neurons were also DP.
source: While deceleration prediction disproportionately characterized neurons not active at transition (χ2(1, n=1565)=24.33, p<0.0001, Figure 3B), most transition-active neurons were also DP (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Neurons selectively active while BIL or BID at transitions showed both sensitivity to zone and a predominance of DP among zone-discriminating neurons at the transition moment.
source: Comparison of neurons exclusively active while BIL or else selectively active while BID at transitions illustrated both sensitivity to zone, as well as a predominance of DP among zone-discriminating neurons at the transition moment (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Neurons which appear to best discriminate zone transition based on acute shifts in relative valence are also DP neurons.
source: Thus, neurons which appear to best discriminate zone transition based on acute shifts in relative valence are also DP neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the calcium imaging data.

claim: These data support a role for patchy neurons in locomotor restraint during LDb transitions.
source: These data support a role for patchy neurons in locomotor restraint during LDb transitions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the calcium imaging data.

claim: A significant difference existed in patchy neuron activity surrounding transitions into light versus dark zones.
source: A significant difference existed in patchy neuron activity surrounding transitions into light versus dark zones (GLME fixed effects 95% CI (a.u.) in brackets: ∆F/F is increased by BIL for approach [0.39086, 0.78166] and retreat [0.35765, 0.75611], Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by GLME analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Peak ∆F/F during transition into dark occurred while BIL, but did so early in the approach, below half-maximal speeds.
source: Peak ∆F/F during transition into dark occurred while BIL, but did so early in the approach, below half-maximal speeds (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mean R-values representing the direction of correlation between ∆F/F and speed for each animal indicate a negative correlation to acceleration exclusively during transition into the light zone.
